newsitem.title: UK: Physical Sugar - EU whites stay firm for quality.
newsitem.headline: Physical Sugar - EU whites stay firm for quality.

text.p: Premiums for European Union (EU) white sugars are holding steady with support seen from north African offtake and sustained demand for quality cargoes after a spate of Polish deliveries, market sources said on Thursday.

Libya, Algeria and Tunisia have all bought white sugar over the last few weeks, while market sources said Iran may have bought as much as 170,000 tonnes of European 45 ICUMSA whites over the past few weeks.
More Middle East offtake is expected before the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan, due to start in mid-January.
Elsewhere, a number of freight orders have emerged specifying Mauritania as an end destination, and market sources said Gambia was interested in buying 20,000 tonnes of whites.
Traders quoted EU cargoes from Antwerp at between $10 and $12 over March futures for Dec/Jan shipment, with other north European ports such as Rostock commanding much lower premiums.

Activity in Antwerp was said to be bustling, with prices supported by a good volume of parcel-sized shipments. Although European freight rates are now picking up, the lower levels seen recently had encouraged buying of EU cargoes, traders said.

London's freight market has also seen inquiries for European ports which are not so often quoted, such as Motril and Santander, but brokers said Antwerp might even be cheaper as high port costs made shipments from these ports very expensive.
But the sugar situation in Poland has also been a key factor affecting the strength of the EU premium.

Polish ports were specified for deliveries of 9,900 tonnes of 60 ICUMSA white sugar at the expiry of London's December futures contract. In the October expiry, Polish ports accounted for the total delivery of 14,050 tonnes.

"The argument is that Polish sugars are going to bring the value of the tape down...it's just more availability and maybe people will value EU sugars at a premium to the tape," said Chris Pack, senior analyst at Czarnikow Sugar.

"Because of the terms of the (London No.5) contract, flat tape is for premium sugars and therefore most of the whites are normally valued at a discount, either because they're 100s or because they're just less desirable," he said.

While Polish sugar just qualifies as deliverable under the contract terms, its quality was still below that of the bulk of the supply -- EU sugar -- and so the quality of the market's deliverable cargoes was reduced to the lowest specification.
More Polish sugar is expected to feature in the London expiries next year, which traders will try to avoid because of its lower quality.
"Poland will have sugar for export and that will be the sugar delivered into the tape at the March and May expiry," said one physical broker.
He said the worst possible scenario would be to receive Polish sugar with European sugar elsewhere valued at $4 or $5 above the Polish price.
This premium of EU over Polish sugars was not likely to fall in the short term and would probably rise, he added.

In its latest monthly report, trade house E D & F Man said the total amount of sugar to exported from Poland's expected surplus was still unclear as the government had still to decide the amount of sugar to be taken into state reserves.
Poland could have an export surplus of as much as 400,000 tonnes from its 1996/97 beet crop but has only authorised 118,300 tonnes for export subsidies, it said.
The government has now said it wants to raise the quota for domestic sugar sales by 130,000 tonnes to 1.63 million tonnes to help absorb the surplus.

EU producers also have to contend with 45 ICUMSA availability from north Brazil and Thailand, apart from the stream of whites expected to emerge from Saudi Arabia's new refinery at Jeddah when it enters production early next year.
Traders quoted Thai cargoes for February/March at $12 over March futures and north Brazilian cargoes ex-Recife at a discount of between $7 and $4 for December/January.
